paragraphs: The paper examines different mathematical ways to represent a system that evolves in discrete time. Its starting point is operator models used in linear signal processing when numerical values have limited precision. It brings these models into a common framework so that their relationships can be understood and their use in neural network modeling can be compared.

The comparison concerns the gamma, delta, and rho operator models. The application is nonlinear system identification and prediction: learning a description of a system's behavior and using that description to predict its outputs. Here, the representation of time-dependent behavior is part of the modeling choice, alongside the neural network that learns the relationship.

The authors also introduce a model built around an adaptive bilinear transformation that generalizes all three operators. This makes the contribution both comparative and unifying: existing alternatives become instances of a broader construction. The stated result is this shared formulation and new generalization, rather than a claim that one named operator consistently produces the best predictions.
neurips-1994-a-comparison-of-discrete-ti.tldr: The paper unifies three discrete-time operator models and introduces an adaptive generalization for neural network system identification and prediction.

paragraphs: AutoTypist aims to reduce typing by predicting the next word and letting the user accept it with one keystroke. The system takes advantage of repeated word choices and predictable text structure. Its interaction is straightforward: the user continues composing, while the network offers a likely continuation that can replace several individual keystrokes.

A multilayer perceptron generates the predictions. It adapts both to the user's word usage and to the characteristics of the text being written. This makes the prediction task sensitive to the person and the current material, rather than treating every writing situation as having the same likely vocabulary or sequence of words.

The authors report typing-speed improvements of 2–3% for English prose and 10–20% for C code, with comparable reductions in keystrokes. The larger programming gains show that the demonstrated benefit depends on the material. They also suggest annual time savings exceeding 20 hours per user and possible reductions in repetitive strain injuries; those are potential consequences of the measured typing savings.
neurips-1994-a-connectionist-technique-f.tldr: AutoTypist learns a user's typing patterns to suggest next words, producing larger demonstrated speed gains for C code than for English prose.

paragraphs: The paper develops a theory of how songbirds learn to imitate a tutor's song through coordinated auditory and motor learning. The goal is to explain both the acquisition of vocal behavior and response properties observed in neurons across several brain nuclei involved in song learning. This connects a learning algorithm to a proposed biological mechanism.

The central proposal assigns a learning role to the anterior forebrain pathway. This pathway is essential for acquiring song even though adult birds do not need it to produce an established song. The model suggests that it supplies changes at synapses together with adaptive evaluations, allowing syllable production to be adjusted through reinforcement.

A computer implementation reproduced a real zebra finch song with 90% accuracy according to a spectrographic measure. A second-generation model reached 96% accuracy in matching the tutor song. These results show that the proposed framework can generate close acoustic matches. They support its usefulness as a computational account while remaining distinct from direct confirmation of the proposed neural learning mechanism.
neurips-1994-a-novel-reinforcement-model.tldr: A reinforcement learning model links a proposed birdsong learning pathway to simulations that closely reproduce a tutor's song.

paragraphs: The paper applies reinforcement learning to a pursuit-and-evasion game between a missile and a plane. Time, states, and actions are continuous, while the dynamics are linear and the cost is quadratic. These assumptions define the particular control problem and provide an optimal solution against which the learned behavior can be compared.

The method uses the residual gradient form of advantage updating. It keeps separate estimates of a state's value and the relative benefit of taking an action there. The authors modify the control algorithm to seek a minimax solution, reflecting the opposing objectives of the two players rather than optimizing for a single decision maker.

In simulations, the learned solution converges to the optimal answer. Comparisons include residual gradient and non-residual gradient versions of advantage updating and Q-learning. Advantage updating converges faster in every reported simulation and continues to converge across time-step durations, while Q-learning fails as the steps become small. The findings connect the choice of learning representation to performance when a continuous-time problem is implemented through discrete updates.
neurips-1994-advantage-updating-applied-.tldr: Advantage updating reaches the optimal simulated pursuit-and-evasion solution faster than Q-learning and remains effective as time steps shrink.

paragraphs: The paper constructs an actor/critic learning algorithm that is equivalent to Q-learning and proves its convergence. In an actor/critic arrangement, the actor represents how actions are selected and the critic represents their evaluation through a value function. The contribution connects this division of responsibilities to a learning method expressed through state-action values.

The equivalence comes from encoding Q-values jointly within the actor's policy and the critic's value function. The two components therefore carry information that Q-learning represents in another form. This is a deliberate mathematical construction, so the connection is stronger than an observation that two independently designed methods sometimes learn similar behavior.

The resulting updates have two distinctive features. The critic changes only when the most probable action in the current state is taken. The actor receives reinforcement according to criteria involving the relative probability of the action actually chosen. These rules are central to the construction. The paper's significance is the demonstrated equivalence and convergence of this particular actor/critic algorithm.
neurips-1994-an-actor-critic-algorithm-t.tldr: The paper proves convergence for an actor/critic algorithm constructed to encode and reproduce Q-learning.

paragraphs: The paper describes an analog chip for locating sounds and translating their positions into coordinates suitable for eye movements. This addresses a sensorimotor problem: information from hearing and vision must be expressed in a compatible frame to guide orientation toward an event. The superior colliculus motivates the design because its deeper layers contain spatially organized responses to multiple senses.

The proposed hardware localizes sound in the azimuthal plane, corresponding to direction around the listener. It extends an architecture associated with barn owl auditory localization to a primate eye movement system. That extension requires an additional transformation because auditory position is treated as head-based, whereas the visual representation is tied to the retina.

The coordinate transformation is intended to model the pathway from auditory cortical areas to deeper layers of the primate superior colliculus. The chip is interfaced with an analog hardware system for rapid eye movements being developed in the same laboratory. Its contribution is a concrete implementation connecting sound localization, coordinate conversion, and an eye movement interface.
neurips-1994-an-auditory-localization-an.tldr: An analog chip combines sound localization with the coordinate transformation needed to guide a primate-inspired eye movement system.

paragraphs: The paper asks when combining several least-squares estimators improves regression predictions. It separates expected error into bias and variance so that the consequences of combination can be examined individually. Bias concerns systematic mismatch in what is learned, while variance concerns how much the learned result changes with the available sample.

The authors compute exact bias and variance curves as sample size changes. Their calculations identify a setting where combination is particularly useful: a small, noisy dataset and a target function that the available model cannot represent exactly. This last condition, called unrealizability, matters because additional training data cannot by itself remove the model's representational mismatch.

The benefit does not persist uniformly across sample sizes. In the analyzed setting, a single estimator performs better with large datasets. The authors also show that dividing data into independent subsets and training a different estimator on each can sometimes improve performance substantially. Together, these findings make combination a choice whose value depends on data quantity, noise, and representational fit.
neurips-1994-bias-variance-and-the-combi.tldr: Exact bias–variance calculations show when combining least-squares estimators helps and when a single estimator performs better.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of applying a speech recognizer trained for one speaker to a new speaker. It places a neural network before a speaker-dependent, hidden Markov model recognizer. This front end maps the new speaker's acoustic spectra to reduce differences between speakers before recognition takes place.

The mapping uses a generalized resource allocating network with local, elliptical Gaussian units and an additional linear term. Units are allocated recursively, and parameters are optimized online. This gives the spectral mapping an adaptable structure while allowing its parameters to change as acoustic data arrives. The reported normalization uses 40 sentences chosen to provide broad phonetic coverage.

On the APASCI continuous speech corpus, the method reduces phone recognition errors and reports an adaptability ratio of 25%. That figure is the stated adaptation measure, rather than a claim of 25% overall recognition accuracy. The results compare favorably with a multivariate linear mapping using constrained orthonormal transformations, supporting the usefulness of this neural front end for speaker adaptation.
neurips-1994-connectionist-speaker-norma.tldr: An adaptive neural spectral mapping improves speaker-dependent speech recognition for a new speaker using 40 phonetically rich sentences.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning problems in which an observation arises from the interaction of several independent underlying factors. Its aim is to discover that structure from data without supervised labels. Representing observations through multiple contributing factors makes the learning problem one of identifying combinations of causes and how they account for the observations.

The authors derive a learning algorithm for the cooperative vector quantizer architecture using expectation-maximization. In this framework, the expectation step evaluates possible hidden explanations of the data, and learning uses those evaluations to update the model. The central obstacle is combinatorial: considering the possible combinations of factors makes the exact expectation step computationally intractable.

Two alternatives address that obstacle: Gibbs sampling and a mean-field approximation. They offer different ways to make the otherwise unmanageable step computable within the learning procedure. The paper presents promising empirical results for these approaches. Its contribution is therefore both a principled learning formulation and practical approximate methods for carrying it out when exact hidden-factor calculations are too expensive.
neurips-1994-factorial-learning-and-the-.tldr: The paper derives an EM-based method for learning interacting hidden factors and approximates its intractable expectation step.

paragraphs: The paper explores how a learning system can use knowledge beyond a collection of input-output examples. Its approach, learning from hints, incorporates additional information about the target relationship into the same learning process. The hints may express common-sense rules or specialist knowledge that would otherwise remain outside the training examples.

The motivation is financial market data, where noisy observations can make the intended relationship difficult to learn. Hints give the learner another source of guidance about that relationship. The idea is to make available knowledge part of training, allowing observed examples and other information about the target function to contribute together.

The authors demonstrate the approach in foreign-exchange trading involving the U.S. dollar against the British pound, German mark, Japanese yen, and Swiss franc over 32 months. They also explain how to apply the general method to other markets. Although neural networks provide the starting context, the learning model is not restricted to them. The contribution is a method for incorporating knowledge and a financial application demonstrating its use.
neurips-1994-financial-applications-of-l.tldr: Learning from hints incorporates expert or common-sense knowledge into training and is demonstrated on foreign-exchange trading.

paragraphs: The paper integrates hierarchical mixtures of experts into a continuous speech recognizer based on hidden Markov models. The change concerns how the system estimates probability densities. Instead of using Gaussian mixtures for this part of the recognizer, it uses many relatively small neural networks arranged in a hierarchy.

The hierarchy resembles a decision tree, but its decisions are soft: contributions need not be confined to a single hard choice. Another distinction is that the parameters of all the neural networks can be trained automatically using expectation-maximization. These properties make the hierarchy a trainable probability-estimation system within the larger speech recognition architecture.

The authors report results using the 5,000-word and 40,000-word Wall Street Journal speech tasks. These applications place the method in continuous speech recognition with two vocabulary sizes. The main stated contribution is the integration itself: a hidden Markov model can retain its overall recognition framework while using a hierarchy of neural experts as its density estimator. The abstract does not state a comparative performance gain.
neurips-1994-hierarchical-mixtures-of-ex.tldr: The paper replaces Gaussian mixture density estimation in an HMM speech recognizer with a trainable hierarchy of neural experts.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what people learn when practicing reaching movements in an unfamiliar mechanical environment. The experiments indicate that practice builds an internal model of inverse dynamics: a mapping that connects a desired movement to the commands needed under the environment's mechanical conditions. This frames motor learning as acquiring a usable computational model.

Participants recalled the learned model when tested 24 hours after initial practice. The experiments also examined what happens when another mapping is learned immediately afterward. When the new mapping was anticorrelated with the first, learning showed interference. The relationship between the two mappings therefore mattered for how successfully the second could be acquired.

The authors interpret this interference as evidence that the two mappings draw on the same computational elements in memory. Reusing those elements to encode the second mapping could disrupt what they previously represented. They consequently predict forgetting of the initially learned skill. The observed recall and interference establish the behavioral findings, while shared computational elements and resulting forgetting form the proposed explanation and prediction.
neurips-1994-interference-in-learning-in.tldr: Reaching experiments show retained inverse-dynamics learning and interference between opposing mappings, suggesting shared motor-memory resources.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a neural network can learn better by solving several related tasks together. Its starting idea is that good generalization depends on capturing regularities underlying a domain. Learning tasks jointly gives the network multiple sources of evidence about those regularities, rather than relying on the training signal from a single task.

The proposed approach uses backpropagation to train the related tasks at the same time. Each task provides an inductive bias for the others: it influences which patterns the learner is encouraged to represent. The paper extends the idea that domain information can enter learning through network outputs by making related prediction tasks a source of that guidance.

The authors identify five mechanisms through which multitask backpropagation improves generalization and provide empirical evidence from real domains. The stated finding is that joint learning can improve performance beyond the training examples. Relatedness is central to the argument because the tasks are intended to inform one another about useful structure in the domain.
neurips-1994-learning-many-related-tasks.tldr: Training related tasks together lets them guide one another's representations and can improve neural network generalization.

paragraphs: The paper focuses on limits to classification accuracy that come from the database itself. Random errors and insufficient information can constrain a classifier both when it learns from the database and when it is applied to it. This makes the quality of the available evidence part of the prediction problem, alongside the learning method.

The authors propose a method for estimating the limiting performance imposed by that evidence. The quantity of interest is a ceiling associated with the database, rather than simply the score achieved by a particular trained classifier. Such an estimate gives a way to reason about how much room the available information leaves for improved predictions.

The technique is demonstrated on predicting failures in telecommunication paths. This application grounds the data-quality question in a concrete classification task. The paper's contribution is the proposed estimate of attainable performance and its demonstration. Its central implication is that assessing a learning system requires considering the errors and insufficiencies in the data on which its decisions depend.
neurips-1994-limits-on-learning-machine-.tldr: The paper proposes estimating the accuracy ceiling imposed by database quality and demonstrates it on telecommunication failure prediction.

paragraphs: The paper considers data expressed as pairwise dissimilarities: information about how different items are from one another. Two goals are to visualize those relationships and to organize the items into groups. The authors treat these as difficult combinatorial optimization problems associated with multidimensional scaling and pairwise clustering.

Their discussion places several algorithms within a maximum entropy framework. One task embeds the dissimilarity data in Euclidean space, giving the items a geometric representation. Another clusters them to reveal group structure. A third actively selects data that will help the clustering process. These tasks address different parts of understanding the same relational information.

Active selection is especially relevant when some of the data remains unknown. Instead of requiring all relationships to be available before seeking structure, the approach chooses information to support the clustering process as it proceeds. The stated contribution is a framework covering representation, grouping, and information selection, with active selection offering a strategy for efficiently discovering structure from partially known data.
neurips-1994-multidimensional-scaling-an.tldr: The paper connects dissimilarity visualization, clustering, and active data selection within a maximum entropy framework.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to describe movement through a smaller collection of reusable components. It builds on Optimal Unsupervised Motor Learning, a theory in which a network discovers a reduced-order controller for an unknown nonlinear system. The reduction comes from representing the system's most significant modes rather than retaining every possible component.

The extension applies this idea to sequences of commands. The important components now correspond to movement primitives: patterns that can be combined to produce different motions. This shifts the representation toward the structure of movements over time. A collection of such primitives provides the ingredients for generating a wider variety of movements through combination.

The author demonstrates the approach in decomposing and synthesizing human handwriting and in analyzing movements elicited by stimulation of the frog spinal cord. These applications connect the theory to both constructing movement and interpreting movement-related experiments. The contribution is a common way to discover significant components of command sequences and use them as building blocks for understanding or producing motion.
neurips-1994-optimal-movement-primitives.tldr: An extension of unsupervised motor learning discovers movement primitives that can be combined to analyze and synthesize motions.

paragraphs: The paper tackles classification with many possible classes by splitting it into decisions between pairs. For each pair of classes, a neural network learns using only examples belonging to those two classes. Each subproblem therefore has a narrower distinction to learn, and its network can potentially be relatively small.

The key contribution is a method for combining those pairwise outputs into posterior probabilities for the complete classification problem. The system must turn separate two-class judgments into probabilities over the available classes. Producing these probabilities gives the combined classifier more information to report than a collection of unrelated pairwise decisions.

The resulting classifier forms part of a handwriting recognition system used for reading checks. The authors evaluate it on real-world databases and report results that compare favorably, from a practical standpoint, with other neural network approaches. The paper thus connects a decomposition strategy to a probability-producing recognition system, showing how specialized two-class networks can contribute to a single multiclass decision in an applied setting.
neurips-1994-pairwise-neural-network-cla.tldr: Pairwise neural classifiers are combined into multiclass posterior probabilities and applied to handwriting recognition for check reading.

paragraphs: The paper compares neural networks with logistic regression for predicting death, stroke, and renal failure after coronary artery bypass surgery. The study uses records from 1,257 patients at the Lahey Clinic. Both approaches receive the same input features, and evaluation uses 50 bootstrap replications to assess performance across resampled data.

The neural models are sigmoid multilayer perceptrons with either no hidden layer or one hidden layer. They are trained with stochastic gradient descent and early stopping. The authors report slightly better risk prediction overall, with mortality ROC areas of 76.0% for the networks and 70.5% for logistic regression using preoperative features. These areas concern discrimination between outcomes, rather than the percentage of patients classified correctly.

Early stopping provides regularization and is identified as an important contributor to the improvement. The paper also develops an auxiliary confidence network that learns to reproduce prediction intervals derived from 50 bootstrap-trained networks. This adds a way to approximate the uncertainty information produced by the collection of fitted models.
neurips-1994-predicting-the-risk-of-comp.tldr: Neural networks modestly improve surgical complication risk prediction, with early stopping helping performance and an auxiliary network estimating confidence intervals.

paragraphs: The paper presents neural network feedback control of a high-temperature plasma in a tokamak fusion experiment. Strong magnetic fields confine the plasma, and controlling its boundary requires adjustments to the magnetic field structure. The control task concerns both the plasma's position and its shape, with feedback needed within a few tens of microseconds.

Software simulations show significantly better performance from the neural network approach than from the linear technique described as common in tokamak experiments. This motivates using a learned nonlinear approach for the control task. The simulation comparison establishes the reported performance advantage, while the paper also presents results from using neural networks in real-time plasma control.

Meeting the timing requirement requires specialized hardware. The authors develop a fully parallel multilayer perceptron implementation combining digital and analog technology. The work therefore links a control method to the hardware needed to execute it quickly enough. Its practical importance lies in bringing neural computation into a feedback loop whose usefulness depends on both control quality and response time.
neurips-1994-real-time-control-of-a-toka.tldr: A parallel neural network implementation enables real-time tokamak plasma control, with simulations showing advantages over a conventional linear technique.

paragraphs: The paper addresses decision problems in which the environment is Markov but the learner cannot observe its complete state. Restricted observations mean the information available to the learner may not support the usual Markov assumptions. Consequently, algorithms and analyses built around fully accessible state information cannot generally be carried over unchanged.

The proposed algorithm combines Monte Carlo policy evaluation with a policy improvement procedure resembling that used in Markov decision problems. It searches over stochastic policies, which assign probabilities to actions rather than always selecting one fixed action for a given observation. In this setting, such policies can perform considerably better than any deterministic policy.

The authors analyze the method and guarantee convergence to a local maximum. That guarantee concerns a locally optimal policy, rather than necessarily the best policy in the entire search space. Although action probabilities create a continuous search space even when the action choices are discrete, the algorithm remains computationally tractable. The contribution is a learnable, analyzed approach for this class of restricted-observation problems.
neurips-1994-reinforcement-learning-algo.tldr: The paper introduces a tractable stochastic-policy learning algorithm with local convergence guarantees for a class of partially observable problems.

paragraphs: The paper extends reinforcement learning methods from discrete-time Markov decision problems to semi-Markov decision problems, a continuous-time generalization. The central issue is how to preserve useful learning ideas when the timing structure of decisions changes. The authors begin by reviewing the semi-Markov setting and the corresponding version of Bellman's optimality equation.

They then propose adaptations of temporal-difference learning, Q-learning, and real-time dynamic programming. These methods draw on asynchronous dynamic programming and stochastic approximation: updating estimates through successive computations or observations rather than requiring a complete solution at once. The adaptation connects these established learning approaches to the optimality conditions of the continuous-time setting.

The algorithms are demonstrated on the task of finding an optimal controller for a simple queueing system. This supplies a concrete decision problem for examining how the extensions operate. The paper also discusses circumstances in which they may be useful. Its contribution is a set of learning formulations for semi-Markov problems and an illustrative control application, rather than a stated ranking of the methods.
neurips-1994-reinforcement-learning-meth.tldr: The paper adapts several reinforcement learning algorithms to semi-Markov decision problems and demonstrates them on queueing control.

paragraphs: The paper tackles a gap between reinforcement learning theory and the compact representations needed for larger problems. Lookup tables store information separately for states, but practical learning often requires a smaller representation. The authors investigate how function approximation can be combined with reinforcement learning while retaining a mathematical account of convergence.

Their approximation method extends state aggregation, which groups states to reduce representation size. Soft aggregation makes the grouping non-discrete, allowing a more flexible relationship between states and aggregates. The authors develop convergence theory for arbitrary but fixed soft aggregation and offer an interpretation of how aggregation affects learning as experience arrives.

They also propose a heuristic that adapts the aggregation to find improved compact representations. It exploits the flexibility of soft membership rather than treating grouping as a purely discrete decision. Preliminary empirical results accompany the method. A crucial distinction is that the stated convergence theory applies to fixed aggregation, while the adaptive procedure is presented as a heuristic for improving the representation.
neurips-1994-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Soft state aggregation provides compact reinforcement learning representations, convergence theory for fixed groupings, and a heuristic for adapting them.

paragraphs: The paper proposes that parietal cortex represents spatial information in a form that supports multiple sensorimotor transformations. The key ingredients are an object's retinal location and the position of the eyes. Together, these can provide information from which different coordinate descriptions are constructed, rather than requiring a single dedicated spatial frame.

The authors model a neuron's response as a Gaussian function of retinal position multiplied by a sigmoid function of eye position. A collection of these responses forms a set of basis functions. They show that simple linear transformations of this representation can generate receptive fields expressed either relative to the retina or relative to the head.

The proposal also yields a prediction about hemineglect following parietal damage. If the underlying representation serves several coordinate transformations, neglect should appear in multiple reference frames within one patient. The authors report that several experiments support this prediction. The contribution connects a mathematical representation of neuronal responses to both flexible spatial computation and an observable consequence of brain injury.
neurips-1994-spatial-representations-in-.tldr: A basis-function model explains how parietal activity could support multiple spatial reference frames and predicts multi-frame hemineglect.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to translate neural network weights into symbolic rules. Such rules can help explain network behavior, and the authors note that symbolic descriptions may also improve generalization in some domains. The central problem is to connect a unit's numerical parameters with a meaningful logical expression in a principled way.

The method uses weight templates: parameterized regions of weight space associated with particular symbolic expressions. With an appropriate representation, template parameters can be identified and instantiated to find the optimal match to a unit's actual weights. This makes rule extraction a structured matching problem between learned numerical behavior and available symbolic forms.

The supported rule families have different computational costs. Arbitrary conjunctions and disjunctions can be handled in O(k), where k is the number of inputs. Simple and recursive n-of-m expressions require O(k!) under the stated method. These expressions describe threshold-like combinations of conditions. Simulations across several problems demonstrate effectiveness, while the complexity results make the cost of choosing richer rule forms explicit.
neurips-1994-template-based-algorithms-f.tldr: Parameterized weight templates extract symbolic rules from neural units, with explicit computational costs for different rule families.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for directing visual attention toward regions that matter for a task. Its central representation is a saliency map over the input retina. Each region's importance is understood in relation to the task being performed, making spatial selection part of how the system handles visual information.

The map is created through predictive auto-encoding. This connects the learned predictive representation to the decision about where attention should be focused. The map supplies a spatial indication of useful input, allowing the attention mechanism to identify relevant portions of a scene even when other features compete strongly for attention.

The authors demonstrate the method on two simple tasks containing multiple strong distracting features. These demonstrations address whether the attention approach can function in the presence of conspicuous competing information. The paper also presents possible architectural extensions and application directions. Its stated contribution is an implemented, simple mechanism for task-relevant spatial attention, supported by initial demonstrations in deliberately distracting visual inputs.
neurips-1994-using-a-saliency-map-for-ac.tldr: Predictive auto-encoding creates a task-relevant saliency map that guides visual attention in demonstrations with strong distractors.
